SAINT model: trend of a reference population and stationary spreads

Source: R/model-saint.R
saint.Rd

The SAINT model (Spread Adjusted InterNational Trend) of Jarner and Kryger (2011) in the revised form of Jarner and Jallbjørn (2022). It forecasts the adult mortality of small populations as deviations (spreads) from the trend of a large reference population. The trend carries the long-term development. The spreads are stationary, so the populations do not diverge from the reference.

Usage

saint(
  reference,
  by = NULL,
  ecm = NULL,
  spread_ar = "diagonal",
  background = TRUE
)

Arguments

reference

Reference strata: stratum labels, or a named list of values of stratum variables, for example list(region = "Deutschland").

by

Stratum variable(s) with a trend each, for example "sex". NULL: one trend for all strata.

ecm

NULL, or the group of by whose mean changes give the common drift of the error-correction model that couples the level and slope of two trends (Section 5.2.1), for example "female". Needs by with two groups.

spread_ar

A of the VAR(1) of the spread: "diagonal" (diagonal, estimated, 0 <= A_ii <= 0.99), "full" (unrestricted, eq. 5.12), or a number a in [0, 1) for A = a I (the paper's choice for Denmark: 0.99).

background

Whether the trend has the background mortality exp(zeta_t) of eq. 5.3 (default). FALSE leaves it out, a model of the class of Section 4.2, which allows empty components. Use it where the data do not identify a background, for example rates smoothed over age; a warning says when the estimate of the background reaches its lower bound, which makes its random walk and the forecasts at young ages unstable.

Value

A model specification (joint over strata).

Details

The reference is one or more strata of the data (reference), for example the national total or several countries. Their deaths and exposures are pooled into one reference population (Jarner and Kryger 2011, Section 3.1). With by (for example "sex"), each group gets its own trend; both papers fit women and men separately. All other strata of a group are targets with a spread from the group's trend. A group with a single reference stratum forecasts that stratum by the trend. In a group with several reference strata, each of them is also a target, as Jarner and Kryger (2011, concluding remarks) propose for a group of related populations.

Version

This is the version of Jarner and Jallbjørn (2022), the model in use at the Danish pension fund ATP. Its authors replaced three components of the original model: the deterministic parametric trend by a stochastic frailty model, so that forecasts describe the uncertainty of the trend (Section 2.2); the trend's age pattern by one that fits high ages better (Section 2.4); and the three spread regressors (level, slope, curvature) by five (Section 5.4). Section and equation numbers below refer to Jarner and Jallbjørn (2022) unless the 2011 paper is named.

Trend (Sections 4 and 5.1)

The reference rates are mu(t, x) = exp(-sigma2 M(t, x)) mu0(t, x) + exp(zeta_t) (eqs. 5.1-5.3), with baseline log mu0(t, x) = alpha_t + beta_t (x - 75) + kappa_t (x - 75) 1{x < 75} (eq. 5.2), background mortality exp(zeta_t), and Gamma-distributed frailty with mean 1 and variance sigma2 (Example 4.1). exp(-sigma2 M) is the mean frailty of the survivors of a cohort, where M(t, x) cumulates the observed rates of the cohort, background subtracted, from the first age of the data; years before the first year take the rates of the first year (eqs. 4.7-4.8). Deaths are Poisson (eq. 4.9). For a given sigma2, the indexes of every year are the estimates of the EM algorithm of Appendix B; sigma2 maximises the profile pseudo-likelihood (eq. 4.14). kappa and zeta follow random walks without drift (eq. 5.4). alpha and beta follow a bivariate random walk with drift (Section 4.5) or, with ecm, the error-correction model of Section 5.2.1 for two groups (eqs. 5.5-5.6): the equilibrium differences are the differences at the jump-off year and the common drift is the mean change of the group named by ecm (women in the paper). The median forecast is then a random walk with this drift for both groups, and in every path the differences between the groups stay stationary. Rates are forecast by eqs. 4.15-4.17: the mean frailty follows from the baseline cumulated along each cohort. Selection by frailty makes the rates of improvement at high ages rise over time (Section 3.3).

Spread (Section 5.4)

A target's rates are the trend times exp(y_t' r(x)) (eq. 5.10), with regressors r_i(x) = min(1, max(0, x_i - x) / 20) and knots x_i = 40, 60, 80, 100, 120 (eq. 5.11). The spread parameters y_t of each year are Poisson maximum likelihood estimates given the fitted trend (eq. 5.9); the trend is estimated first and kept fixed, the two-stage estimation of Jarner and Kryger (2011, concluding remarks). They follow a VAR(1) model without mean, y_t = A y_{t-1} + u_t with normal innovations (eq. 5.12), so the spread reverts towards zero. spread_ar sets A; the paper recommends a diagonal A with 0 <= A_ii < 1 and imposes A = 0.99 I for Denmark, a deviation half-life of about 69 years (Section 5.4.1). Each target has a VAR(1) of its own, "a separate VAR model" per target population (Section 5.4.1).

Forecasts and uncertainty

Draws include the innovations of the trend indexes and of the spread. Trend and spread are independent (Jarner and Kryger 2011, eq. 5). Parameters are fixed, as in Jarner and Kryger (2011, Section 2.3.3), who leave parameter uncertainty aside. Forecasts start from the fitted rates of the last year; the paper uses no jump-off correction (2022, Section 5.3). Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) add Poisson variation of the deaths given the rates, the observation model of the papers.

Ages

Both papers use single ages 20-100 and model adult mortality only (2011, Section 1.2). saint() needs consecutive single-year age groups from age 20 without an open interval: the frailty term follows cohorts year by year. Ages below 20 are refused. Ages above 100 are accepted; the parametric trend extends to them (2022, Section 5.1.1). Drop an open interval with mt_subset(x, ages = c(20, 100)); estimate single years from age groups with mt_ungroup() or step_ungroup().

Corrections and package-specific choices

Three formulas of Jarner and Jallbjørn (2022) are read as evident misprints. In (B14) and (B16) the denominator c F - G is the rate c F + G of (B7)-(B8). In the second line of (4.16) the baseline of year t_max is that of year t - 1. The common drift of Section 5.2.1 divides the sum of changes by t_max - t_min + 1; the package divides by the number of changes, the empirical average that the text describes.

Package-specific (reference unknown):

  • the fixed point of the EM algorithm is computed by Newton-Raphson sweeps (Fisher scoring) over the parameters of each year with the mean frailty held fixed, alternated with updates of the mean frailty; Section 4.4 names Newton-Raphson as the alternative to EM, and the tests check that both give the same estimates;

  • sigma2 is searched from 0 by doubling (0.025, 0.05, ..., 3.2) and then by stats::optimize() around the best value; a warning (class mt_warning_saint) is given at the upper end;

  • starting values, and a lower bound of 1e-10 on the background rate, with a warning when it binds (see background);

  • on age ranges narrower than 20-100: kappa is set to 0 without ages on both sides of 75, and spread regressors that are 0 at all ages, or 1 at all ages like the level, are left out;

  • the innovations of kappa and zeta are independent of each other and of alpha and beta (the paper gives their marginal distributions), and the spread innovations of different targets are independent; variances are maximum likelihood estimates;

  • the adjustment coefficients and the innovation covariance of the error-correction model are Gaussian maximum likelihood estimates given the equilibrium differences and the drift; a warning is given when the model does not correct deviations (eigenvalues of eq. 5.8 outside (-1, 1));

  • spread_ar = "diagonal": each A_ii is the least-squares coefficient of its component, bounded to [0, 0.99] (a warning names the strata where 0.99 binds); "full": conditional maximum likelihood (the 2011 paper uses Yule-Walker estimates of the same model), with a warning when A is not stationary.

background = FALSE is an opt-in variant of this package: the SAINT specification of Section 5.1 has a background, the class of models of Section 4.2 allows it to be left out.

Not implemented: the deterministic trend and the three regressors of 2011, the error-correction model with free equilibrium and drift, and frailty distributions other than Gamma (Appendix A).

References

Jarner SF, Kryger EM (2011). Modelling adult mortality in small populations: the SAINT model. ASTIN Bulletin 41(2): 377-418. doi:10.2143/AST.41.2.2136982

Jarner SF, Jallbjørn S (2022). The SAINT model: a decade later. ASTIN Bulletin 52(2): 483-517. doi:10.1017/asb.2021.37

See also

li_lee() and coherent_fdm(), other models whose strata keep bounded distances to a common trend.

Examples

x <- mt_example_regions(years = 1995:2019, regions = 3, ages = "single")
h <- mt_hierarchy(region = "all", quintile = "all")
x <- mt_aggregate_strata(mt_subset(x, ages = c(40, 100)), h)
x <- mt_subset(x, quintile == "all", drop = TRUE)
fit <- mt_fit(saint(reference = list(region = "all"), by = "sex"), x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
p <- mt_parameters(fit)
p[parameter == "sigma2"]
#>         stratum parameter  index       value
#>          <char>    <char> <char>       <num>
#> 1: trend female    sigma2        0.000000000
#> 2:   trend male    sigma2        0.002233368
